name: Whitening powder (charcoal)

lead: Charcoal whitening powder is brushed onto teeth to lift surface stain, one of several consumer whitening formats alongside strips, pens and rinses. People use it for cleaner, lighter-looking teeth.

Proponents say the charcoal adsorbs and abrades stain from the enamel. It does not bleach internal tooth colour. Only a laboratory study of a related charcoal toothpaste and mouthwash on stained teeth was identified; no human trials were found.

paras: Users dip a damp brush in the powder and brush for a minute or two, a few times a week, sometimes alternating with regular toothpaste.
Whitening toothpastes in general contain more abrasives than regular ones, and the effect of charcoal on enamel has been examined in vitro. No clinical safety data were found.

angle.text: Users brush on activated charcoal powder to adsorb and abrade surface stain for cleaner, lighter-looking teeth, as one of several consumer whitening formats. Research on it is limited to laboratory work.

lead: Charcoal whitening powder is activated charcoal sold as a fine black powder that people brush onto their teeth to lift surface stain from coffee, tea and similar sources. The aim is a brighter-looking smile, and charcoal powders sit alongside strips, pens, rinses and whitening toothpastes among consumer whitening formats.[1][2]

Proponents say the charcoal adsorbs pigments and works as a mild abrasive, so stained enamel looks lighter after brushing. A British Dental Journal review describes charcoal toothpastes and powders as fashionable products used for tooth brushing, extrinsic stain removal and, as claimed, whitening, and notes that dental teams are often asked about them and answer largely from experience rather than trial data.[2]

Research is small but exists. A 2024 randomized clinical trial compared charcoal powder and charcoal toothpaste with regular fluoride toothpaste and 10% carbamide peroxide; the charcoal products produced whitening comparable to regular toothpaste, with carbamide peroxide giving the largest change.[3]

paras: Users usually apply the powder with a wet toothbrush or fingertip. Wikipedia notes that whitening toothpastes in general contain more abrasives and detergents than regular pastes to help remove stain, while peroxide-based products change tooth color by bleaching.[1]
Charcoal products are marketed in powder, toothpaste and mouthwash forms in many countries, including the UK, US, Japan, India, Thailand, Australia, Hong Kong, China and Korea.[2]

On looksmax.org, a thread asks whether charcoal can clean teeth; one reply suggests whitening strips instead because they are faster, and another says charcoal is corrosive and can wear enamel if used often.[4]

A 2020 in vitro study stained forty human canines with coffee and compared brushing with deionised water, regular toothpaste and charcoal-containing products over a simulated 90 days for color change and enamel surface alteration.

A 2023 randomized laboratory trial brushed aged resin composite specimens with a charcoal dentifrice or whitening toothpastes for 14 minutes. Surface roughness did not differ significantly between groups, though roughness rose after brushing within each group.[5]

A single-blind randomized trial in 56 volunteers (four groups of 14, 14 days of treatment) compared activated charcoal powder, charcoal toothpaste, fluoride toothpaste and 10% carbamide peroxide. Charcoal products whitened to a degree similar to regular toothpaste; carbamide peroxide gave the best result and highest satisfaction. The authors called the charcoal effect minor and unsatisfactory.[3] Beyond this trial, published clinical data on charcoal powders are limited, and the 2019 review noted the lack of strong evidence behind manufacturers' claims.[2]

lore.intro: Charcoal powder is discussed on looksmax.org as a home alternative to whitening strips, with members raising questions about whether it works and whether it abrades enamel.[4]
